context:
SUGGESTED ANGLE: Only 630 million years after the Big Bang, a black hole already weighed about 360 million Suns, yet it is feeding slowly now. So how did it get that big so fast? Euclid found this cosmic monster among millions of dots, and it broke Euclid's own record set just four months earlier.
- ESA's Euclid space telescope discovered the quasar J1504+6252, nicknamed Dún Aonghasa, at redshift 8.13. It is seen as it was just 630 million years after the Big Bang. (SOURCE: https://www.esa.int/articles/about-us/directorates/science/euclid/euclid-breaks-own-quasar-record-by-40-million-years)
- The discovery breaks Euclid's own previous quasar record by looking back in time an additional 40 million years. (SOURCE: https://www.esa.int/articles/about-us/directorates/science/euclid/euclid-breaks-own-quasar-record-by-40-million-years)
- Dún Aonghasa is the first quasar identified beyond a redshift of 8. (SOURCE: https://www.esa.int/articles/about-us/directorates/science/euclid/euclid-breaks-own-quasar-record-by-40-million-years)
- The team picked the quasar out of millions of objects in about 18 months of Euclid survey data. (SOURCE: https://www.esa.int/articles/about-us/directorates/science/euclid/euclid-breaks-own-quasar-record-by-40-million-years)
- The quasar is powered by a black hole with a reference mass of about 360 million solar masses. (SOURCE: https://arxiv.org/html/2611.31385)
- Medium-resolution JWST/NIRSpec G395M spectroscopy gave a systemic redshift of z = 8.129 ± 0.005. (SOURCE: https://arxiv.org/html/2611.31385)
- The paper uses Keck/MOSFIRE and LBT/LUCI ground-based spectroscopy as part of confirming the quasar. (SOURCE: https://arxiv.org/html/2611.31385)
- Julien Wolf led the discovery team. He was at the Max Planck Institute for Astronomy and is now at the European Southern Observatory (ESO). (SOURCE: https://phys.org/news/2026-11-quasar-tightens-constraints-black-hole.html)
- The black hole's mass falls between about 210 million and 780 million solar masses, with 360 million as the reference value. (SOURCE: https://phys.org/news/2026-11-quasar-tightens-constraints-black-hole.html)
- The black hole is feeding relatively slowly, which means it must have grown rapidly at an earlier stage. (SOURCE: https://www.techtimes.com/articles/331465/20261124/most-distant-quasar-found-euclid-telescope-slow-feeding-black-hole-needed-rapid-early-growth.htm)
- The quasar is named after Dún Aonghasa, a prehistoric cliff-top fort on Inis Mór in the Aran Islands, off Ireland's Atlantic coast. (SOURCE: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D%C3%BAn_Aonghasa)
- In July 2026, Euclid reported 31 new quasars at 6.6 < z < 7.8. The most distant of them, EUCL J1729, at z ≈ 7.77, was then the most distant quasar ever discovered. (SOURCE: https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2026/07/aa58883-26/aa58883-26.html)
- The two record-setting quasars from July 2026, EUCL J172902.75+641018.1 and EUCL J125308.55+705432.3, are at redshifts 7.77 and 7.69. (SOURCE: https://www.astronomy.com/science/euclid-spots-the-oldest-known-quasars/)
- Euclid can detect quasars 10 to 100 times fainter than earlier searches could. (SOURCE: https://www.min.uni-hamburg.de/en/ueber-die-fakultaet/aktuelles/2026/0706-euclid-entdeckt-aelteste-quasare-im-universum.html)
- ESA expects at most a few tens of quasars beyond redshift 8 across Euclid's entire survey. (SOURCE: https://www.esa.int/articles/about-us/directorates/science/euclid/euclid-breaks-own-quasar-record-by-40-million-years)
